source.title: Unsupervised Feature Discovery via Simple Clustering

record.tranche_reason: The study tests clustering as a method for discovering interpretable, causally influential activation groups, but does not test superposition, capacity pressure, polysemanticity, or the listed claims about SAE features and feature dimensionality.
record.gate_note: The distinguishability and patching results below concern clustering-based feature discovery, an adjacent topic rather than a listed claim version. The paper also reports a qualitative cluster analysis; those results are recorded as findings that fit no version. Figure 5's per-configuration values are not given in the text, so only the stated approximate comparison is recorded.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether recursive k-means clustering of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct layer-20 activations yields interpretable, causally active directions. It never measures superposition, feature overlap, capacity competition, polysemanticity, or SAE completeness, stability or canonicity. The SAE run is only a baseline for the clustering method's distinguishability score.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct: the authors conclude that clustering can recover features, with interpretable clusters and causal effects from centroid patching. However, the paraphrase's statement that they present this as not testing superposition is the reader's framing; the authors never mention superposition at all.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses recursive binary k-means clustering of normalized model activations, rather than the method in Toy Models of Superposition. It evaluates cluster examples against an SAE baseline and uses activation patching.
record.method_sensitivity: The distinguishability result changes with tree level: the authors say accuracy is near-perfect already at level 6 and improves only slightly at deeper levels. The text does not provide exact per-level values.

fits_no_version.finding: Clusters from recursive k-means on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct layer-20 activations are judged coherent (≈97% actual-vs-decoy accuracy). Patching in a centroid direction redirects continuations in two examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Simple clustering of LLM activations recovers interpretable, causally active directions, competitive with SAE features on example coherence.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-20 examples of SAE features (matryoshka-65k) are distinguishable from decoys at ≈79%, which the authors attribute to long-tail low-activation examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Example coherence of SAE features under an LLM-judge eval depends on how many candidate examples each feature has.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; submitted as part of Neel Nanda's MATS Application
record.problems: The qualitative cluster analysis is anecdotal. The paper's per-level distinguishability values are shown in a figure but not stated numerically in the text; the reported accuracy uses an LLM judge. Patching evidence consists of two illustrative examples, with no reported aggregate across prompts or clusters.

untested.parts: All: toy models, overlap and near-orthogonality of features, sparsity-dependent transition, geometry.
All: capacity competition, dedicated versus shared dimensions, polysemantic neurons.
Whether features are spread across neurons, and whether an SAE recovers sparse features. The SAE is used only as a baseline.
SAE completeness, stability and canonicity. The conclusion mentions seed instability only as future work.
The dimensionality of features. Cluster centroids are assumed to be 1-D directions by definition.

missing.what: Per-configuration distinguishability accuracies for tree levels 6–11. These are shown only in a figure and are method-performance values, not version-relevant.

record.verdict_notes: A single-author LessWrong MATS application post. The SAE comparison is confounded by unequal candidate depths, and the patching evidence consists of two anecdotes. No version of the claim is tested, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Not tested: feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular superposition geometry.
Not tested: capacity competition, dedicated versus shared dimensions, or polysemanticity.
Not tested: alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity evidences superposition.
The study evaluates interpretability of SAE-feature examples, but does not test whether LLM features are spread across neurons or whether a dictionary recovers sparse features in the sense claimed.
Not tested: SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
Not tested: whether superposed features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Qualitative inspection of clusters at the first tree level
rows.measure: Human-observed semantic and lexical coherence of activation examples
rows.value: The paper reports examples organized around lexical categories (including adjectives, verbs, and nouns) and semantic categories (including place names, biomedical material, and drug codes).
rows.note: Qualitative observation; does not measure superposition or any listed version.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Qualitative inspection of a cluster subtree
rows.value: The paper identifies child clusters as objects, spaces, concepts, and groups; it also says the earlier split separates physical from social/abstract things. It notes that some splits are not meaningful, including verbs split across both children.
rows.note: Reports both coherent and non-coherent qualitative subdivisions; no quantitative measure.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Qualitative inspection of chained cluster assignments
rows.measure: Coherence of activation examples for chained clusters
rows.value: The paper reports coherent examples for combinations of clusters labeled as verbs and prepositions, and says such chains often yield coherent examples.
rows.note: Qualitative finding about clustering, not a test of a listed claim version.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Actual-versus-decoy distinguishability evaluation of Motio cluster examples
rows.measure: Judge accuracy identifying the actual cluster's set of examples
rows.value: Approximately 97% (reported in the abstract for Motio clusters); the text says accuracy is near-perfect at the first tree level and improves only slightly at deeper levels.
rows.note: The text does not give exact values for each tree level; this result measures cluster-example coherence, not a listed version.
rows.check: This is the study's own method (Motio clusters) scored against an SAE baseline, a method-performance result rather than a measure of any version. The ≈97% figure is from the abstract; per-level values appear only in Figure 5.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Actual-versus-decoy distinguishability evaluation of SAE feature examples
rows.measure: Judge accuracy identifying the actual SAE feature's set of examples
rows.note: The paper suggests the long tail of low-activation SAE examples may confuse the judge; this is not a test of SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
rows.check: This is the SAE comparator in a method comparison. The ≈79% is confounded by candidate depth: about 39 candidates per SAE feature versus ≈161k per cluster, as the authors note. It does not test V4 or V5.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Replaced the last-token residual-stream activation after block 20 with a cluster-centroid direction scaled to the original activation's distance from the dataset mean
rows.measure: Generated continuation after patching compared with untouched decoding
rows.baseline: Untouched decoding continues in the java.* namespace
rows.value: Patched decoding instead continues in the org.* namespace
rows.note: One of two illustrative patching examples; the paper reports the qualitative change in continuation.
rows.check: The state 'observed' refers only to the patching effect on the continuation; the row bears on no version. It is a single illustrative example with no aggregate rate.

rows.note: Illustrative patching example; the study does not report a quantitative rate across prompts or clusters.
